title: What do you say?
hook: "Zeno said this," but what do you say? Stop only quoting (Letters 33)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Socrates. Your line was a change of soul. Which one habit did you shift, right where you were? Day four hundred fifty-eight.

Here's an odd thing to hear on a path that has been quoting old teachers for over a year. Lucilius has been enjoying the short, sharp sayings Seneca tucks at the end of his letters, mostly lines from Epicurus. He asks for more. And in the thirty-third letter, Seneca says, in effect: no. Not because the sayings are bad. Because Lucilius is old enough now to have his own. It's the moment a teacher gently takes away the training wheels, and it might be aimed at us too. Today: what do you say?
screen: `LUCILIUS ASKS FOR MORE QUOTES.` → `SENECA SAYS NO.` → `THE TRAINING WHEELS COME OFF.`

segments.voice: First, why the Stoics don't do highlights. Epicurus' school, Seneca says, puts a few brilliant lines up front. The Stoic writers are different: the good is spread all through, so plucking out single flowers misses the field. Second, the age for notebooks. It's fine for a child to learn a few sayings by heart, he says. But for a grown man to lean only on a notebook of other people's lines is embarrassing. Then comes the jab that gives us today's title. Zeno said this. And you? Cleanthes said that. And you? How long will you march under someone else's command? Third, the people who only interpret. Seneca grumbles about those who never write anything of their own, but always hide in another's shadow, explaining. Remembering, he says, isn't the same as knowing. Remembering is holding something someone gave you to keep. Knowing is making it yours. Fourth, the guides. The great teachers who went before, he says, are not our masters but our guides. The truth is open to everyone, and plenty of it is still left for those who come after. That's the posture this path hopes for. We've listened to Epictetus, to Seneca, and we'll listen to Marcus. Sooner or later, though, the question turns around. Not what did they say. What do you say?
screen: `THE STOICS DON'T DO HIGHLIGHTS.` · `ZENO SAID THIS. AND YOU?` · `REMEMBERING ISN'T KNOWING.` · `GUIDES, NOT MASTERS.` · then, large: `WHAT DO I SAY?`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one idea from these letters that has stuck with you. Maybe the water clock, or start poor, or change your soul, not your sky. Now let go of Seneca's words for it. How would you put it, in your own plain words, to a friend over coffee? Try a sentence silently. Then try it again, simpler. When it feels like yours, write it down, or just hold it. The bell holds the time.
Zeno. Seneca's challenge: Zeno said this, Cleanthes said that, but the teachers are guides, not masters, and the next line is yours. Today's word.
Your line: what do I say. Write one line of your own today, about anything you've learned on this path. No quotation marks. Keep it somewhere you'll see it. Day four hundred fifty-eight.

howItsDone: Some readers of the Stoics keep a notebook where, after copying a teacher's line, they try to restate it in their own words and test it against their own life.

fork.setup: you're Lucilius, a grown man, and you ask Seneca for another batch of quotations. what does he send?
options: a challenge: Zeno said this, and you?
fork.reveal: Seneca tells him to stop marching under someone else's command and start speaking for himself.

original.note: Latin, Seneca, Letters 33.11: not our masters, but our guides.

trapdoor: what you thought: quoting the greats is how you show you've learned.
what it means: the teachers are guides; at some point you have to say it in your own words.
what a scholar hears: Letters 33.7 ('hoc Zenon dixit: tu quid?') and 33.11 ('non domini nostri sed duces sunt'); Seneca says learning sayings by heart suits children, not a grown student.
